nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: An IS auditor must conclude on the operating effectiveness of an access-review control across a full year. Which sampling approach provides the BEST statistical basis for projecting results to the population?
choices: Judgmental sampling of high-risk users only
Sampling only the first and last month of the year
Sampling whichever review records the system owner provides
Statistical (random) sampling sized to the desired confidence and precision
questions.explanation: Only statistical sampling lets the auditor extrapolate results to the population with measurable confidence and precision — exactly what is needed to conclude on operating effectiveness over a full period. Judgmental sampling is not projectable; period-end-only sampling misses interim failures; and relying on management's selection introduces bias and breaches auditor independence.

questions.q: An IS auditor must conclude on the integrity of a financial application's transaction log. Which evidence is the MOST reliable?
choices: A signed letter from the application owner confirming the log is intact
Hash values produced by an independent forensic tool comparing two snapshots
A screenshot taken by the developer showing recent transactions
A verbal walkthrough from the database administrator
questions.explanation: ISACA ranks evidence by independence and objectivity: independently computed hash values produced by a tool outside the audited party's control sit at the top of the hierarchy. Owner letters, developer screenshots and DBA walkthroughs are all representations from interested parties and can be selectively prepared, so they carry materially lower reliability.

questions.q: When drafting the annual IS audit plan, engagement selection should be based PRIMARILY on:
choices: Areas where the auditee has explicitly requested coverage
The IS audit team's familiarity with the technology in scope
A documented IT risk assessment ranking auditable units
Whatever areas were covered in the prior-year plan, for continuity
questions.explanation: ISACA's standards require the annual plan to be risk-based, with engagements prioritised against a current, documented IT risk assessment of the auditable universe. Auditee preference, prior-year coverage and auditor comfort all skew the plan away from the highest-risk areas and toward what is convenient rather than what matters most.

questions.q: An IS auditor reviews the IT steering committee charter. Which composition BEST supports IT governance objectives?
choices: Senior business executives, the CIO and the CFO, chaired by a business executive
Only the CIO, CTO and head of infrastructure operations
The CIO and a rotating group of project managers from active initiatives
The CEO alone, making all IT investment decisions on the committee's behalf
questions.explanation: Effective IT governance demands that IT investments be steered by the business. A committee that includes senior business executives alongside the CIO and CFO — and is chaired by a business leader rather than the CIO — keeps decisions tied to business value and risk appetite. An IT-only committee biases decisions toward technology, project managers operate at delivery level, and CEO-only decision-making bypasses the deliberative review the committee is meant to provide.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A small organisation cannot fully segregate database administration from application development. Which compensating control is MOST effective?
flashcards.back: When segregation of duties is infeasible, the strongest compensating control is detective: an independent reviewer monitors the privileged user's activity logs with alerts on sensitive actions, so misuse is detected promptly. Mandatory leave and role rotation are periodic and miss anything done between cycles, and password complexity does nothing to constrain an authorised privileged user.

flashcards.front: An IS auditor is engaged during the design phase of a new application. The auditor's PRIMARY role is to:
flashcards.back: ISACA stresses auditor independence: the auditor advises and assesses but does not own control design, approve solutions or write tests, because any of those activities would create a self-review conflict at later audit. The proper role during design is to provide independent assurance that the proposed controls map to the documented risks the project is meant to mitigate.

flashcards.front: An IS auditor reviewing change management finds that emergency changes bypass the standard change advisory board (CAB) approval workflow. The BEST recommendation is to:
flashcards.back: Emergency changes are a legitimate operational need; banning the path is unrealistic and pushes fixes underground. ISACA's expectation is a controlled fast-track: the change is applied to restore service, then formally reviewed and approved retrospectively by the CAB within a defined window. Unbounded documentation deadlines and self-approval defeat the control's purpose entirely.

flashcards.front: An organisation has set an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours for its order-entry system. Which strategy MOST efficiently meets BOTH objectives?
flashcards.back: A 1-hour RPO requires data to be replicated at least hourly, and a 4-hour RTO requires infrastructure that can be brought online comfortably within that window. Hourly log shipping satisfies the RPO and a warm standby satisfies the RTO. Nightly tapes already blow the RPO by up to 24 hours, weekly NAS backups blow it further, and same-data-centre snapshots violate site-diversity requirements for credible DR.

questions.q: A small organisation cannot fully segregate database administration from application development. Which compensating control is MOST effective?
choices: Requiring the DBA to take annual mandatory leave
Rotating the DBA role between two staff every six months
Independent review of DBA activity logs with alerting on privileged actions
Increasing the password complexity requirements for the DBA account
questions.explanation: When segregation of duties is infeasible, the strongest compensating control is detective: an independent reviewer monitors the privileged user's activity logs with alerts on sensitive actions, so misuse is detected promptly. Mandatory leave and role rotation are periodic and miss anything done between cycles, and password complexity does nothing to constrain an authorised privileged user.

questions.q: An IS auditor is engaged during the design phase of a new application. The auditor's PRIMARY role is to:
choices: Take responsibility for designing the application's internal controls
Approve the final design before construction work may begin
Develop the test scripts that will be executed during user acceptance testing
Assess whether the proposed controls will adequately address identified risks
questions.explanation: ISACA stresses auditor independence: the auditor advises and assesses but does not own control design, approve solutions or write tests, because any of those activities would create a self-review conflict at later audit. The proper role during design is to provide independent assurance that the proposed controls map to the documented risks the project is meant to mitigate.

questions.q: An IS auditor reviewing change management finds that emergency changes bypass the standard change advisory board (CAB) approval workflow. The BEST recommendation is to:
choices: Eliminate the emergency change path so every change goes through the standard CAB
Require emergency changes to be formally reviewed and approved by the CAB post-implementation
Allow the on-call engineer to document the change at their next convenience
Delegate emergency change approval to whichever person raises the ticket
questions.explanation: Emergency changes are a legitimate operational need; banning the path is unrealistic and pushes fixes underground. ISACA's expectation is a controlled fast-track: the change is applied to restore service, then formally reviewed and approved retrospectively by the CAB within a defined window. Unbounded documentation deadlines and self-approval defeat the control's purpose entirely.

questions.q: An organisation has set an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours for its order-entry system. Which strategy MOST efficiently meets BOTH objectives?
choices: Hourly transaction log shipping plus a warm standby server at the DR site
Nightly tape backups shipped offsite each morning
Weekly full backups stored on a local NAS in the production data centre
Quarterly snapshots replicated to a second rack in the same data centre
questions.explanation: A 1-hour RPO requires data to be replicated at least hourly, and a 4-hour RTO requires infrastructure that can be brought online comfortably within that window. Hourly log shipping satisfies the RPO and a warm standby satisfies the RTO. Nightly tapes already blow the RPO by up to 24 hours, weekly NAS backups blow it further, and same-data-centre snapshots violate site-diversity requirements for credible DR.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: The MOST important indicator that an organisation's backup strategy will succeed during a real disaster is:
flashcards.back: A "success" status only confirms a job ran — organisations regularly discover at recovery time that the resulting backups were unreadable, partial or missing critical data. ISACA emphasises that only documented, successful restore tests against the stated RPO and RTO actually prove recoverability. Library capacity and encryption strength are useful operational concerns but say nothing about whether the data can be brought back.

flashcards.front: A corporate laptop containing customer records is stolen from an employee's car. Which control would have BEST limited the data exposure?
flashcards.back: Once a device is physically in attacker hands, only cryptographic protection of the data at rest meaningfully limits exposure: full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication keeps the contents unreadable without the key. BIOS passwords are trivially bypassed by removing the disk, the AUP is an administrative control with no protective effect against a thief, and antivirus addresses malware on a running system rather than physical loss.

flashcards.front: An IS auditor reviewing user access in a financial system finds that 18 terminated employees retain active accounts up to 90 days after their departure. The BEST recommendation is to:
flashcards.back: The root cause is a process gap between HR and identity management. The strongest fix drives deactivation from the authoritative HR system, so terminations close access immediately and consistently. Quarterly certifications and manager emails are compensating controls that still leave gaps measured in weeks or months, and extending log retention has no preventive effect on the access remaining active.

flashcards.front: A financial reporting application is reachable from the public internet using only a username and password. Which control would MOST effectively reduce the risk of account compromise?
flashcards.back: Credential phishing and password reuse defeat any password-only scheme regardless of length or rotation. Multi-factor authentication with a phishing-resistant factor (for example FIDO2 security keys) breaks the attack chain even when the password is known to the attacker. Frequent rotation actually weakens password quality in practice, raw length still falls to phishing, and time-based restrictions are trivially circumvented by attackers operating from another time zone.

questions.q: The MOST important indicator that an organisation's backup strategy will succeed during a real disaster is:
choices: The number of backup jobs that report a "success" status each night
The total capacity of the offsite media library
Documented evidence of successful periodic restore tests against defined objectives
The strength of the encryption algorithm used on the backup media
questions.explanation: A "success" status only confirms a job ran — organisations regularly discover at recovery time that the resulting backups were unreadable, partial or missing critical data. ISACA emphasises that only documented, successful restore tests against the stated RPO and RTO actually prove recoverability. Library capacity and encryption strength are useful operational concerns but say nothing about whether the data can be brought back.

questions.q: A corporate laptop containing customer records is stolen from an employee's car. Which control would have BEST limited the data exposure?
choices: A strong BIOS password protecting the boot sequence
A signed acceptable-use policy acknowledged by the user at hire
Antivirus software with up-to-date signature definitions
Full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication
questions.explanation: Once a device is physically in attacker hands, only cryptographic protection of the data at rest meaningfully limits exposure: full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication keeps the contents unreadable without the key. BIOS passwords are trivially bypassed by removing the disk, the AUP is an administrative control with no protective effect against a thief, and antivirus addresses malware on a running system rather than physical loss.

questions.q: An IS auditor reviewing user access in a financial system finds that 18 terminated employees retain active accounts up to 90 days after their departure. The BEST recommendation is to:
choices: Integrate the joiner-mover-leaver process with HR so departures trigger automatic account deactivation
Run a quarterly access certification campaign covering all users in the system
Require managers to email the IT helpdesk whenever a member of their team leaves
Lengthen the audit log retention period so missed departures can still be detected later
questions.explanation: The root cause is a process gap between HR and identity management. The strongest fix drives deactivation from the authoritative HR system, so terminations close access immediately and consistently. Quarterly certifications and manager emails are compensating controls that still leave gaps measured in weeks or months, and extending log retention has no preventive effect on the access remaining active.

questions.q: A financial reporting application is reachable from the public internet using only a username and password. Which control would MOST effectively reduce the risk of account compromise?
choices: Forcing users to change their passwords every 30 days
Increasing the minimum password length to 16 characters
Requiring multi-factor authentication using a phishing-resistant factor
Restricting interactive logins to local business hours only
questions.explanation: Credential phishing and password reuse defeat any password-only scheme regardless of length or rotation. Multi-factor authentication with a phishing-resistant factor (for example FIDO2 security keys) breaks the attack chain even when the password is known to the attacker. Frequent rotation actually weakens password quality in practice, raw length still falls to phishing, and time-based restrictions are trivially circumvented by attackers operating from another time zone.
